newsitem.title: USA: Nextel sees Q2 digital growth ahead of plan.
newsitem.headline: Nextel sees Q2 digital growth ahead of plan.

text.p: Nextel Communications Inc's recently launched national digital wireless network is seeing rapid user growth in excess of analysts' expectations in the second quarter, the company's President said.

Speaking at a PaineWebber technology conference here, Timothy Donahue, who is also the company's chief operating officer, said that the success of Nextel's business oriented digital network leads him to believe that the company will turn cash flow positive ahead of schedule.
Nextel's stock was the second most actively traded stock in late Thursday afternoon trading, rising 1-1/4 to 16.
Donahue said the Nextel digital network is growing in excess of the 150,000 net new subscribers analysts have forecasted for the current quarter ending in June.
"I will tell you that we will exceed that in the second quarter," he said.
By contrast, the company added 122,000 units in the first quarter, ending the period with 422,900 subscribers. The company's older analog wireless network has about 700,000 users.
"The growth in the second quarter has been gratifying to say the least," Donahue said.
"We had a hell of a first quarter and we are going to have a hell of a second quarter," the executive said.
He attributed the accelerating growth, in part, to a national $35 million TV, radio and print advertising campaign the company began in early April.

Nextel reported first quarter revenues of $111 million versus $68 million in the same quarter a year ago. The company's net loss widened in the first quarter to $0.93 per share versus a loss of $0.56 a year ago.
The Nextel executive said he now sees the company becoming cash flow positive in the third quarter of 1998, ahead of the company's original plan to enter positive cash flow territory in 1999.
"I would say you are probably looking at third quarter 1998," Donahue said in response to an audience member's question.
He cautioned that if the company changes course and begins to target the consumer market and not just corporate customers, the turning point in cash flow could be delayed.
Donahue said the company has no plans to enter the U.S. consumer market as the costs of acquiring customers do not currently generate enough revenue to make such an effort worthwhile.
He said the company's average revenue per unit is $59, well ahead of the cellular industry's $48 per unit.
He added that the average business user is spending $70 to $75 per month with Nextel.

Donahue said he expected the company's average revenue per unit to continue to grow through 1997 and into 1998 as the company aggressively expands its wireless network to serve 300 cities covering 85 percent of the U.S. population.
Currently the company's network covers more than 200 cities.
The company launched its Dallas operation on Wednesday and now covers nine of the top ten U.S. metropolitan markets.
Nextel offers an integrated wireless communications system, based on a GSM-like wireless standard, that includes phone service, paging and voice mail.

The digital wireless service offers higher voice quality than traditional cellular phones, and an innovative feature that allows a traveling user to instantly contact any number of colleagues at the push of a button.

Driving demand for the service is the $0.10 per minute charge that users pay for this direct connection, two-way radio service. In addition, the company has eliminated roaming charges throughout its national network.
The company which is backed by cellular pioneer Craig McCaw and Motorola Inc, has arranged $3 billion to fund the rapid expansion of its U.S. wireless operation.
Donahue said the company has sufficient capital to complete its current expansion plans.
The company is also active in overseas markets in Asia and Latin America through its McCaw International unit.
